care_notes: A single male needs a heated, filtered, lidded tank with a footprint of at least 45x30 cm; bettas breathe air at the surface, so surface area matters more than depth. They need a heater — Seriously Fish gives 22-30 C and Aquarium Co-Op targets around 27 C, and unheated rooms below 22 C cause lethargy and infection. Feed a betta-specific pellet once daily, only as much as it eats in about a minute. Never house two males together, and add tank mates only in tanks of 38 L or more with heavy planting and escape routes.
common_mistakes: Keeping them in unheated, unfiltered bowls or vases
Assuming the labyrinth organ means they do not need clean water or filtration
Overfeeding, which causes bloating and constipation
Housing with fin-nippers or with other long-finned, brightly coloured fish
Putting two males, or a male and female outside breeding, in one tank
disputed: Minimum volume is commonly cited between 19 L and 40 L. Aquarium Co-Op accepts 5 gal (19 L) as workable and prefers 10 gal (38 L); Seriously Fish specifies a 45x30 cm base, which is about 38-40 L at normal tank heights. We list the larger figure. Temperature also disputed: Seriously Fish gives a wide 22-30 C tolerance, Aquarium Co-Op recommends around 27 C.

care_notes: Guppies are hard-water fish: they want pH above 7.0 and plenty of calcium and magnesium, and they do badly in soft, acidic, RO-based water. Keep two to three females per male, or a single-sex group, otherwise females are harassed constantly. They breed roughly every 30 days and a tank fills fast, so plan for fry or plan to rehome them. Cooler water around 22-24 C extends lifespan; keeping them at 28 C speeds growth but shortens life to about 18 months.
common_mistakes: Keeping more males than females, so females are chased to exhaustion
Soft or RO water without remineralising, causing wasting and fin problems
Not planning for fry, leading to a badly overstocked tank within months
Housing with fin-nippers such as tiger barbs or serpae tetras
Buying heavily inbred fancy strains and expecting them to be as hardy as older stock
disputed: Aquarium Co-Op allows a trio in a 5 gal (19 L) tank but recommends 38-76 L long term; Seriously Fish specifies 45x30x30 cm (about 40 L). We list 40 L. Temperature ranges also differ: Seriously Fish gives 17-28 C tolerance, Aquarium Co-Op recommends 24-26 C.

care_notes: Endlers are smaller and generally hardier than fancy guppies, and tolerate a very wide range of hardness and temperature, including unheated rooms in warm climates. They hybridise freely with guppies and produce fertile offspring, so never mix the two if you care about keeping a pure line. Broods of 5-25 arrive every 23-30 days, so a colony grows quickly. Because of their small size they are best in a species tank or with other nano fish, not a general community.
common_mistakes: Keeping them with guppies, which produces hybrids and destroys both lines
Housing them with fish large enough to eat them
Not accounting for exponential colony growth in a small tank
Assuming they need heated tropical temperatures everywhere - in most of India they need no heater
disputed: Aquarium Co-Op gives a 5-10 gal (19-38 L) minimum and says room temperature is fine; Seriously Fish specifies 45x30x30 cm (about 40 L) and a warmer 24-30 C. We list 38 L and a range spanning both temperature positions.

care_notes: Platies are one of the genuinely easy beginner fish: peaceful, hard-water tolerant, and happy anywhere from 20-28 C. Keep at least two females per male or the females are harassed. They produce 20-50 fry a month once mature, and will also hybridise with swordtails if both are present. They need vegetable matter in the diet, not just protein flake.
common_mistakes: Buying only males and females at random rather than a 1:2 or 1:3 ratio
Ignoring the breeding rate until the tank is overstocked
Keeping them in soft water without mineral supplementation
Uncovered filter intakes that suck in fry
disputed: Aquarium Co-Op suggests 10-20 gal (38-76 L); Seriously Fish specifies 60x30x30 cm (about 54 L). We list 54 L as the floor.

care_notes: Mollies are the largest of the common livebearers - females reach 12 cm - and they are hard-water fish that fail in soft, acidic tanks. Most stock is farmed in brackish or heavily mineralised water, and moving them into soft tap water stresses the kidneys and triggers ich, fungus and 'shimmying'. Add crushed coral or a mineral supplement if your GH is below 10. They need a genuine vegetable component in the diet, and a 90 cm tank because they are large, active grazers.
common_mistakes: Keeping them in soft water, the single biggest cause of molly deaths
Adding aquarium salt as a substitute for actual hardness and minerals
Underestimating adult size and buying a 40 L tank for them
Feeding only protein flake with no vegetable matter
Mixing balloon-body strains with normal ones and expecting the same lifespan
disputed: Minimum volume is commonly cited between 76 L and 208 L. Seriously Fish specifies 90x30x30 cm (about 81 L) for the short-finned molly; Aquarium Co-Op says 20 gal (76 L) minimum but 29-55 gal (110-208 L) for larger sailfin types. We list 80 L for P. sphenops and flag that sailfin mollies need substantially more. Some published guides listing 40 gal (151 L) as the minimum for all mollies are conflating sailfin and short-finned types.

care_notes: Swordtails are much bigger than shops imply - females reach 16 cm total length - and they are strong, restless swimmers that need tank length rather than volume. Males form dominance hierarchies and a subordinate male in a short tank gets chased relentlessly, so keep one male with several females or an all-female group. They are hard-water fish like platies and hybridise with them readily. They are accomplished jumpers, so a tight lid is essential.
common_mistakes: Buying them for a 60 cm tank based on the 5 cm juvenile size in the shop
Keeping two or more males in a tank too short for one to escape the other
No lid - swordtails jump out routinely
Soft water, which they tolerate poorly
disputed: This is the largest disagreement in the livebearer set. Seriously Fish specifies a 120x30 cm base (about 108-126 L); most hobby guides and retailers say 20-29 gal (76-110 L). We list 110 L with a 120 cm length requirement, siding with the larger figure because these are fast, long-bodied swimmers.

care_notes: Fancy goldfish are coldwater fish that reach 15-20 cm and live for decades, and they produce far more waste than any tropical fish of the same length. Aquarium Co-Op's rule of 20 gal (76 L) for the first fish plus 10 gal (38 L) for each additional one is the most defensible figure; Practical Fishkeeping's rule of six times adult length by twice adult width gives a similar 90x35 cm footprint. They need no heater in most homes, but they suffer above about 24 C, which matters in much of India - a chiller, a cool room, or simply not keeping goldfish is the honest answer in a 32 C flat. Wide, shallow tanks beat tall ones because oxygen exchange and swimming room both scale with surface area.
common_mistakes: Bowls and 20-40 L 'goldfish tanks', which are the classic beginner killer
Assuming a 3 cm shop fish stays small - they reach 15-20 cm
Adding a heater and keeping them at tropical temperatures
Keeping fancy varieties in strong flow, which they cannot swim against
Housing fancies with fast single-tailed goldfish or comets that outcompete them at feeding
disputed: Minimum volume is commonly cited between 57 L and 150 L for a single fancy goldfish. Aquarium Co-Op says 20 gal (76 L) per fish plus 10 gal (38 L) each additional; Practical Fishkeeping recommends a 60 cm tank as an absolute floor but a 90x30 cm tank for adults. Published figures of 57 L (15 gal) are below every reputable source we checked and should not be used. Temperature is also disputed: Aquarium Co-Op gives 10-21 C, other sources allow up to 24 C.

care_notes: Zebra danios are hardy but they are not nano fish: Seriously Fish specifies a 90x30 cm base because they are relentless, fast swimmers that cover the whole tank all day. They are subtropical, doing best at 18-25 C, and are frequently kept too warm alongside tropical community fish. Keep 8 or more - small groups become nippy and stressed. They jump, so keep a tight lid.
common_mistakes: Selling them as a 20-40 L 'starter tank' fish when they need 90 cm of swimming length
Keeping fewer than 6-8, which turns them into fin-nippers
Keeping them at 26-28 C with tropical fish when they prefer 18-25 C
Housing them with slow or long-finned fish such as bettas and angelfish
Using them to cycle a new tank ('fish-in cycling')
disputed: Minimum volume is commonly cited between 38 L and 81 L. Aquarium Co-Op recommends a 20 gal long (76 L) and a group of 5-6; Seriously Fish specifies a 90x30 cm base (about 81 L) and a group of 8-10. We list 76 L, a 90 cm length, and a group of 8. Temperature: Seriously Fish gives 18-25 C, Aquarium Co-Op 18-24 C - both notably cooler than the 24-28 C many retail tags print.

care_notes: Neons are soft-water fish that prefer the cooler end of tropical - Seriously Fish gives 21-25 C, which is meaningfully below the 26-28 C most community tanks run at, and long-term overheating is a common cause of short neon lifespans. Buy 8-10 at once; smaller groups hide and colour down. They should never be the first fish in a brand-new tank, as farmed stock is prone to neon tetra disease and to crashing in immature water. Dense planting and dim light bring out the colour.
common_mistakes: Adding them to an uncycled or newly set-up tank
Keeping them at 27-28 C long term, which shortens lifespan
Buying 4-6 instead of 8+, so they never school properly
Housing them with angelfish or other fish large enough to eat them as adults
Assuming losses in the first two weeks are normal rather than a sign of poor stock or an immature tank
disputed: Temperature is the key disagreement: Seriously Fish gives 21-25 C, while many retail and hobby sources give 22-28 C. We list 21-26 C and flag that sustained temperatures above 26 C are associated with shortened lifespan. Minimum volume commonly cited between 38 L and 54 L; Seriously Fish's 60x30 cm base (about 54 L) is the figure we use.

care_notes: Cardinals are larger, longer-lived and warmer-water than neons - 23-29 C rather than 21-25 C - so the two are not interchangeable despite looking similar. Much of the stock is still wild-caught from the Rio Negro and arrives stressed, so they need a mature, stable, soft, well-planted tank rather than a new setup. Buy 8-10 minimum. They are micropredators: crushed flake alone is not enough, and they do much better with daphnia, cyclops and baby brine shrimp.
common_mistakes: Treating them as identical to neons and keeping them too cool
Adding wild-caught fish to a tank less than a few months old
Buying small groups, which stresses them and dulls their colour
Keeping them in hard, alkaline water long term
Housing them with angelfish, which eat them once grown
disputed: Minimum volume commonly cited between 54 L and 76 L. Aquarium Co-Op recommends 15-20 gal (57-76 L) for a school of 8-10; Seriously Fish specifies a 60x30 cm base (about 54 L). Difficulty is also disputed: Aquarium Co-Op presents them as a beginner schooling fish, while Seriously Fish's soft-water and mature-tank requirements put them above neons in difficulty. We list intermediate.

care_notes: One of the few genuinely good nano schooling fish - fully grown at 2 cm, so a 45x30 cm tank works for a group of 8-10. They need gentle flow, dim light and dense planting, and their mouths are tiny, so crushed flake, nano pellets and baby brine shrimp rather than standard community food. Colour is dramatically better over a dark substrate in a planted tank. Soft, slightly acidic water suits them best but they adapt to moderately hard water.
common_mistakes: Feeding food too large for their mouths, so they slowly starve in a community tank
Strong filter flow, which exhausts them
Keeping 3-5 instead of 8+
Bare bright tanks, where they stay pale and hide
Housing them with anything big enough to swallow a 2 cm fish
disputed: Minimum volume commonly cited between 19 L and 40 L. Aquarium Co-Op allows a small school in 5 gal (19 L); Seriously Fish specifies a 45x30 cm base (about 38-40 L). We list 38 L.

care_notes: An excellent, genuinely hardy first schooling fish that tolerates a wide temperature and pH range but shows its best colour in soft, slightly acidic, well-planted water. Keep 8-10; in smaller groups they are nervous and stay near cover. Unusually for a rasbora they spawn by gluing eggs to the underside of broad leaves rather than scattering. They are peaceful enough for almost any community tank of similar-sized fish.
common_mistakes: Buying 5-6 rather than 8-10, so they never settle
Bright, bare tanks with no plant cover
Confusing them with the smaller lambchop rasbora (T. espei) and mixing the two groups
Housing them with fish large enough to eat a 5 cm fish
disputed: Minimum volume commonly cited between 38 L and 54 L. Aquarium Co-Op allows a school of six in 10 gal (38 L); Seriously Fish specifies a 60x30 cm base (about 54 L) and a group of 8-10. We list 54 L.

care_notes: The exception among barbs: cherry barbs are genuinely peaceful and safe with long-finned fish, unlike tiger barbs. Males colour up deep red when kept in groups of 6-10 with several females present, and stay washed-out when kept singly or in pairs. They accept a wide pH and hardness range but want dense planting and shade. Endangered in the wild in Sri Lanka, so buy captive-bred stock.
common_mistakes: Assuming all barbs are nippy and excluding them from peaceful communities
Keeping 2-3 fish, so males never develop colour
Buying only males, which then spar constantly
Bright open tanks with no cover
disputed: Minimum volume commonly cited between 38 L and 54 L. Aquarium Co-Op allows a school of six in 10 gal (38 L); Seriously Fish requires a 60x30 cm base (about 54 L) and 6-10 fish. We list 54 L.

care_notes: Tiger barbs are hardy and long-lived but genuinely nippy, and the nipping is worst in small groups and short tanks. A group of 8-12 in a tank of at least 80 cm redirects the aggression within the group; a group of four in a 60 cm tank will shred every long-finned tank mate. Never keep them with bettas, angelfish, guppies or any trailing-finned fish. They are boisterous eaters that outcompete slow, shy species at feeding time.
common_mistakes: Keeping fewer than 8, which turns aggression outward onto tank mates
Housing them with bettas, angelfish, guppies or fancy goldfish
Buying a small group for a 60 L tank
Assuming the aggression is a myth because juveniles in the shop look calm
Adding them to a tank of timid, slow feeders
disputed: Minimum volume commonly cited between 72 L and 110 L. Seriously Fish specifies an 80x30 cm base (about 72 L); Aquarium Co-Op recommends 29 gal (110 L) and a group of at least seven, preferably 12+. We list the larger figure because group size is the main control on aggression. Temperature: Seriously Fish 20-26 C, Aquarium Co-Op 20-28 C.

care_notes: Native across Pakistan, India, Nepal and Bangladesh, and a subtropical fish, not a tropical one: Seriously Fish gives 16-24 C. This is the single most important fact about them and the one most often got wrong - kept at 27-29 C in an unheated Indian tank in summer they are chronically stressed and short-lived. They also get large, to 7.5-10 cm, and need a 100 cm tank and a group of 8-10. Peaceful for a barb, but boisterous enough to bother very small or long-finned fish.
common_mistakes: Keeping them at tropical community temperatures instead of 16-24 C
Buying them for a 60 L tank based on 3 cm juveniles
Small groups, which makes them nippy
Housing them with slow long-finned fish
Assuming the long-finned ornamental strains have the same swimming ability as wild-type
disputed: Adult size is disputed: Seriously Fish says most are fully grown at 6.5-7.5 cm but some forms reach 9-10 cm; Aquarium Co-Op gives 7-10 cm. We list 10 cm. Minimum volume: Seriously Fish requires a 100x30 cm base (about 105 L), Aquarium Co-Op 29 gal (110 L) - these agree. Temperature is where the hobby is most often wrong; we follow Seriously Fish's 16-24 C.

care_notes: Angelfish are cichlids, not community centrepieces: they reach 15 cm long and up to 20 cm tall, so tank HEIGHT matters as much as footprint - aim for at least 45-50 cm of water depth or the fins deform. They eat anything that fits in their mouths, which includes neon tetras, ember tetras and shrimp once grown. Buy six juveniles and let a pair form, then be ready to rehome the rest, because a bonded pair will claim the whole tank when spawning. Warm water, 26-29 C, suits them best.
common_mistakes: Keeping them in tanks under 45 cm tall, which stunts and deforms the fins
Adding neon tetras or shrimp and being surprised when they disappear
Buying two 'to get a pair' and ending up with two fish that fight
Underestimating adult size from a 3 cm juvenile
Housing them with fin-nippers such as tiger barbs, which shred their trailing fins
disputed: Minimum volume commonly cited between 110 L and 200 L. Aquarium Co-Op says 29 gal (110 L) supports up to four adults in a community tank and 55 gal (208 L) for a growing group of 5-6; Seriously Fish says 100x40x50 cm (about 200 L) should be the smallest considered. We list 200 L. Note that both agree height is a hard requirement, which volume alone does not capture.

care_notes: The most peaceful of the large gouramis and far more robust than dwarf gouramis, reaching 12 cm. They are labyrinth breathers and need access to a warm, humid air layer at the surface, so keep the lid on and the water gap small. Males display to each other but rarely do damage if there is space and cover; Practical Fishkeeping suggests two males to four females in a 120 cm tank. They are timid rather than aggressive and get bullied by boisterous tank mates - avoid tiger barbs and other nippers.
common_mistakes: Buying them for a 60 L community tank - they reach 12 cm
Keeping the tank in a cold room with a draughty open top, chilling the labyrinth organ
Housing them with fin-nippers, which target their long pelvic filaments
Keeping multiple males in a short tank with no line-of-sight breaks
Confusing them with the smaller and more disease-prone dwarf gourami
disputed: Minimum volume commonly cited between 81 L and 200 L. Seriously Fish specifies 90x30x30 cm (about 81 L); Practical Fishkeeping recommends a 120 cm tank for a proper group of 2 males and 4 females. We list 110 L with a 100 cm footprint as a middle-conservative figure, and flag that a full group needs 120 cm.

care_notes: Dwarf gouramis are native to the Indian subcontinent and are sold everywhere as a beginner centrepiece fish, but farmed stock carries Dwarf Gourami Iridovirus (DGIV) at high rates - Seriously Fish cites research finding as many as 22% of Singapore-exported fish infected. DGIV is untreatable, usually fatal, and can pass to other species in the same water, so quarantine new fish. Almost all shop fish are male and males are territorial with each other, so keep one per tank unless it is very large. Keep them in a quiet tank with floating plants and gentle flow; they sulk and hide with boisterous tank mates.
common_mistakes: Buying two or three males for one tank, which leads to sustained bullying
Not quarantining, and introducing DGIV to an established community
Assuming a fish that stops eating and develops sores has a treatable bacterial infection
Keeping them in strong filter flow
Choosing them over the hardier honey gourami for a first centrepiece fish
disputed: Minimum volume commonly cited between 38 L and 56 L. Aquarium Co-Op says 10 gal (38 L); Seriously Fish says a 60x30x30 cm (56 L) tank is 'just about big enough for a pair'. We list 56 L. Difficulty is genuinely disputed: Aquarium Co-Op rates them beginner-friendly and reports never seeing DGIV in its own stock, while Seriously Fish treats farmed stock quality as a serious problem. We list intermediate because the disease risk is a stock-quality lottery a beginner cannot assess.

care_notes: Also native to India and Bangladesh, and the better choice over the dwarf gourami for almost every beginner: smaller at 5.5 cm, longer-lived, far less prone to iridovirus, and genuinely peaceful. Not a schooling fish, but they do better in groups of 4-6 where a loose hierarchy forms. They are slow, deliberate feeders and get outcompeted by fast fish such as danios and barbs. Floating plants and dim light bring out the honey colour and reduce shyness.
common_mistakes: Confusing them with the larger, dyed or hybrid 'sunset thick-lipped gourami' sold under the same name
Housing them with fast, greedy feeders that leave them nothing
Keeping them in bright bare tanks with no floating cover, so they stay hidden
Assuming a fish that hides is sick rather than intimidated
disputed: Minimum volume commonly cited between 19 L and 76 L. Aquarium Co-Op says a single fish can live in 5-10 gal (19-38 L) and a group of three does better in 20 gal (76 L); Seriously Fish specifies a 60x30 cm base (about 54 L) for a pair or small group. We list 54 L for a pair and note 76 L for a group of three or more.

care_notes: Footprint matters far more than volume here: corys forage across the substrate all day, so an 80x30 cm base beats a tall 76 L cube. Use fine sand or smooth rounded gravel - sharp or dirty gravel erodes the barbels they feed with, and a barbel-less cory cannot find food. Keep six or more of the SAME species; mixed-species 'cory groups' do not shoal together properly. They must be fed directly with sinking food; they are not cleaners and will not survive on leftovers. They gulp air at the surface occasionally, which is normal.
common_mistakes: Sharp or unclean gravel, causing barbel erosion
Keeping two or three as a 'clean-up crew' instead of a group of six
Assuming they eat algae or leftovers and never feeding them sinking food
Mixing several cory species and counting them as one group
Keeping them at 28 C+ long term, which shortens lifespan
disputed: Minimum volume commonly cited between 54 L and 76 L. Seriously Fish specifies an 80x30 cm base (about 72 L) for long-term care; Aquarium Co-Op recommends 20 gal (76 L). Group size: Seriously Fish says 4-6, Aquarium Co-Op says 6+. We list 6.

care_notes: Kuhlis are burrowers and need soft sand or very smooth fine gravel; on coarse or sharp substrate they cannot bury themselves, stay stressed and can be injured. Keep at least six - kept alone or in pairs they hide permanently and owners assume they died. Feed sinking food after lights-out, since they are largely nocturnal and get outcompeted during the day. They squeeze through any gap, so cover filter intakes and every hole in the lid.
common_mistakes: Keeping one to three, so they never come out and are presumed dead
Coarse or sharp gravel that prevents burrowing
Not feeding them directly, on the assumption they scavenge enough
Uncovered filter intakes and open lid gaps, which they escape into and through
Adding them to a new, unstable tank - they are sensitive to nitrite and to copper-based medications
disputed: Species identity is genuinely unsettled: most fish sold as 'kuhli loach' in the trade are Pangio semicincta or P. oblonga rather than true P. kuhlii, and Seriously Fish has no P. kuhlii profile. Care is effectively identical across the group. Minimum volume commonly cited between 54 L and 76 L: Seriously Fish specifies a 60x30 cm base for P. oblonga; Aquarium Co-Op recommends 20 gal (76 L) for a group of three to six. We list 76 L. Temperature: Seriously Fish 21-26 C, Aquarium Co-Op 23-27 C.

care_notes: This is the pleco to buy instead of a common pleco: it tops out around 10-13 cm rather than 50 cm. It needs real driftwood to rasp on for digestion, plus vegetables and sinking wafers - it will not survive on tank algae alone. Males are territorial with other males and with similarly shaped catfish, so keep one per tank unless it is large with several caves. They breed readily in caves, with the male guarding the eggs, so expect fry in an established tank.
common_mistakes: Buying it as an 'algae eater' and never feeding it, leading to slow starvation
No driftwood in the tank
Keeping two males in one tank
Confusing it in the shop with a juvenile common pleco, which looks similar at 5 cm
Assuming it will keep the glass clean once it is adult - adults eat far more prepared food than algae
disputed: Minimum volume commonly cited between 54 L and 110 L. Seriously Fish says a 60x30 cm base (about 54 L) suffices for a single fish or breeding pair; Aquarium Co-Op recommends 20-29 gal (76-110 L). We list 76 L. Adult size: Seriously Fish 10-12.5 cm, Aquarium Co-Op 10-15 cm.

care_notes: Do not buy this fish for a home aquarium. It is sold at 5 cm as a 'cleaner fish' and reaches over 50 cm, lives 10-20 years, and produces an enormous waste load. Aquarium Co-Op recommends starting at 75 gal (284 L) and moving up to 180 or even 500 gal (680-1900 L); Practical Fishkeeping says tanks of many hundreds of litres are required and criticises its sale for tanks as small as 40 L. Adults are nearly impossible to rehome and must never be released into local waterways, where they are highly invasive. Buy a bristlenose pleco or an otocinclus instead.
common_mistakes: Buying it as an algae eater for a 40-100 L community tank
Believing the myth that a fish grows only to the size of its tank
Not feeding it, so it rasps the slime coat off flat-bodied fish such as goldfish, angelfish and discus at night
Releasing an outgrown fish into a lake or river
Confusing it with a bristlenose pleco at point of sale
disputed: Minimum volume commonly cited between 284 L and 1900 L. Aquarium Co-Op names 75 gal (284 L) as a starting point for a growing fish and 180-500 gal (680-1900 L) for an adult; Practical Fishkeeping declines to give a figure and says 'many hundreds of litres'. We list 680 L as the adult requirement and treat 284 L as juvenile-only. Scientific name is also unsettled - fish sold as 'common pleco' are variously Pterygoplichthys pardalis, P. multiradiatus or Hypostomus plecostomus, and are rarely identified at point of sale.

care_notes: Otos are sold as an easy beginner algae eater but they are the opposite: most are wild-caught, arrive already starving after weeks in transit, and need to graze almost constantly. Only add them to a mature, planted tank at least a few months old that has visible biofilm and soft green algae. Supplement with algae wafers, blanched courgette and cucumber from day one rather than waiting to see if they run out of food. Keep six or more, and expect early losses from imported stock - a group that survives its first two months usually lives for years.
common_mistakes: Adding them to a brand-new tank with no established algae or biofilm
Assuming they will eat the brown or green algae you dislike and nothing else is needed
Buying one or two rather than a group of six
Buying visibly thin fish with sunken bellies
Using copper-based medications, which they tolerate poorly
disputed: Group size is disputed. Seriously Fish recommends at least six; Aquarium Co-Op argues against large groups on the basis that too many otos strip the tank of algae and then starve, preferring a couple of well-fed fish to a starving school. We list 6 and flag that a group is only appropriate in a tank with enough grazing to support it. Minimum volume: Seriously Fish specifies a 45x30 cm base (about 40 L); we list 54 L because the practical constraint is the amount of mature grazing surface, not swimming room. Difficulty: widely sold as beginner; we list intermediate.

care_notes: Rams need genuinely hot water - Seriously Fish gives 27-30 C and Aquarium Co-Op calls 29-30 C the single most important husbandry factor. Kept at the 24-25 C of a normal community tank they slowly decline and die, and this is the most common cause of ram deaths. They also need soft, acidic, pristine water and a mature tank; they are poor competitors and should not go in a busy community. Farmed stock, especially hormone-treated 'electric blue' and 'gold' strains, is often genetically weak with a shortened lifespan. Warm Indian ambient temperatures actually suit this species well.
common_mistakes: Keeping them at standard community temperatures of 24-25 C
Adding them to a tank less than a few months old
Buying a pair from a tank of unsexed juveniles and getting two males
Keeping them in hard alkaline water
Housing them with fast, greedy feeders that outcompete them
Adding dwarf shrimp, which rams hunt
disputed: Minimum volume commonly cited between 54 L and 76 L for a pair. Seriously Fish says a 60x30 cm base (about 54 L) is sufficient for one pair; Aquarium Co-Op recommends 20 gal (76 L) for a pair in a community. We list 76 L. Difficulty is disputed: Aquarium Co-Op rates them moderate, Seriously Fish's requirements (pristine water, 27-30 C, soft acidic, mature tank, poor competitor) put them at advanced. We list advanced.

care_notes: Keep exactly one. Rainbow sharks are solitary and become steadily more territorial as they mature, and both Seriously Fish and Practical Fishkeeping specify a 120 cm minimum tank for a single fish. They are most aggressive toward other bottom-dwelling grazers and toward anything with a similar shape - other rainbow sharks, red-tail sharks, plecos, loaches and corydoras. Provide caves and broken lines of sight. Juveniles hide constantly and look harmless in the shop, which is why they are so often bought for tanks that cannot contain an adult.
common_mistakes: Keeping two or more, which nearly always ends in one fish being killed
Buying one for a 60-100 L community tank based on juvenile behaviour
Housing them with corydoras, loaches, otos or plecos
Assuming they are an algae-eating utility fish rather than a territorial centrepiece
No caves or sight breaks, so the whole tank becomes one territory
disputed: Seriously Fish specifies a 120x45 cm base for a single specimen (about 240 L); Practical Fishkeeping gives 120 cm minimum, keep singly. Many retail guides say 55 gal (208 L) or even 30 gal (110 L). We list 240 L. Both trusted sources agree on the 120 cm length and on keeping them alone.

care_notes: The best algae eater in the hobby for hair algae and black beard algae, and large enough at 5 cm to survive most community fish. They cannot be bred in freshwater - the larvae need brackish or salt water - so every amano in the trade is wild-caught or specialist-raised, and they should be treated as long-lived pets rather than disposable clean-up crew. They need adequate GH and calcium to moult successfully; failed moults are the usual cause of unexplained deaths. Copper-based medications and many plant fertiliser overdoses are lethal to all shrimp. They climb out of open tanks, so use a lid.
common_mistakes: Copper-based fish medications, which kill shrimp at doses safe for fish
Soft, mineral-poor water causing failed moults
Assuming they will eat all algae including green spot algae, which they will not
Keeping them with fish that eat them - large cichlids, goldfish, big barbs
Open-topped tanks - amanos are determined escapers
Overfeeding the fish, after which the shrimp ignore algae entirely
disputed: Neither trusted source states a minimum tank size; Aquarium Co-Op describes them as suitable for 'nano tanks or larger'. We list 20 L as a practical floor because water stability, not swimming room, is the limiting factor. Adult size cited as 4-5 cm across Aquarium Co-Op's two guides. Temperature cited as 18-28 C and 18-27 C.

care_notes: Start with at least 10 so you get both sexes, and expect a colony rather than individuals - they breed continuously in stable, mineral-rich water. They need GH of at least 6 degrees (110 ppm) and KH of at least 2 for successful moulting; soft water is the most common cause of colony collapse. Copper is fatal even at doses used to treat fish, so never medicate a shrimp tank with copper-based products. They live only 1-2 years, so a healthy colony replaces itself; a colony that stops producing young is telling you something about the water. Almost any fish will eat the babies.
common_mistakes: Copper-based medications and some plant fertilisers
Soft or RO water without remineralising for shrimp
Large water changes with mismatched temperature or TDS, which trigger fatal moults
Adding them to a new tank with no biofilm for the babies to graze
Expecting a visible population in a tank with fish that eat shrimplets
Keeping different Neocaridina colours together, which reverts the colony to wild brown in a few generations
disputed: Minimum volume commonly cited between 15 L and 38 L. Practical Fishkeeping gives 15 L as an absolute floor; Aquarium Co-Op recommends a 10 gal (38 L) for a breeding colony. We list 20 L, because for shrimp the risk is water instability rather than crowding, and note that 38 L is a better target for a productive colony. Temperature: both agree on an 18-28 C tolerance with 21-26 C optimal. 'Livebearer' here means direct development - eggs hatch into miniature shrimp with no larval stage.

care_notes: The best algae-eating snail for a freshwater tank: they graze the algal film rather than plants, and will not eat healthy plants. They need hard, alkaline water with real calcium - in soft or acidic water the shell erodes and pits, which is irreversible. Practical Fishkeeping's rule of roughly one snail per 20 L keeps them fed; overstock them and they starve in a tank that looks clean to you. They lay hard white egg capsules on glass, wood and equipment that will not hatch in freshwater but are stubborn to remove. They climb out of open tanks and die on the floor.
common_mistakes: Soft or acidic water, which erodes and eventually breaches the shell
Buying six or more for a small clean tank, so they slowly starve
No lid, so they climb out and dry up
Copper-based medications and salt treatments
Assuming the white egg capsules are a disease or pest
Leaving an upside-down snail on the substrate - they often cannot right themselves
disputed: Minimum volume commonly cited between 8 L and 20 L. Aquarium Co-Op says a nano tank of 2-3 gal (8-11 L) is enough; Practical Fishkeeping's stocking guidance of roughly 20 L per snail implies a larger tank if the snail is to feed itself. We list 20 L. Species identity is loose - 'nerite snail' covers several Neritina and Vittina species sold by shell pattern rather than by name.

care_notes: Mystery snails are pets rather than a clean-up crew - they eat fish food, biofilm, dead plants and dead fish, but will not keep a tank clean. They reach 5 cm and need pH above about 7.2 and GH above 8 degrees (150 ppm) plus calcium-rich food, or the shell grows thin and pitted. Leave a 5-8 cm air gap under a tight lid: they lay pink egg clutches above the waterline and will climb out entirely if there is no gap or no lid. Cooler water extends their short 1-2 year life. Remove them before any copper or salt treatment.
common_mistakes: Soft or acidic water, giving eroded, thin shells
Filling the tank to the rim with no air gap, which they need to breathe and lay eggs
No lid, so they escape and dry out
Copper-based medications and aquarium salt
Housing them with puffers, loaches or assassin snails, which eat them
Assuming a snail sealed in its shell for a day or two is dead
disputed: Naming and taxonomy are genuinely muddled: Aquarium Co-Op lists both Pomacea diffusa and P. bridgesii, and most trade 'mystery snails' are P. diffusa sold under the P. bridgesii name. This matters legally, since some Pomacea species are restricted or banned as invasive in several countries - check local regulations before listing this species by region. Minimum volume: Aquarium Co-Op says 5 gal (19 L); we list 20 L.

care_notes: A hardy, adaptable tetra that fades from black to grey with age — a normal colour change, not a health problem. Can nip fins, especially in too-small a group, so keep 6 or more to spread out any nippiness and avoid pairing with long-finned, slow fish like bettas or fancy guppies.
common_mistakes: Housing with bettas or long-finned livebearers, which it can nip
Keeping too few, which concentrates nipping on one victim

care_notes: A tightly-schooling tetra known for its bright red nose and precise, synchronised swimming in a large enough group — genuinely more sensitive to water quality than beginner tetras like neons, and its schooling behaviour and nose colour are both a reliable indicator of good/poor water. Keep 8 or more; smaller groups school poorly and colour up less.
common_mistakes: Buying only 4-5 and being disappointed by weak schooling behaviour
Adding to an uncycled or poor-quality tank — this species shows water problems fast via faded nose colour and scattering

care_notes: A relative of the piranha that grows to 60-90cm and needs pond-sized housing as an adult — a very common impulse-buy mistake as a small juvenile.
A predatory shoaling fish that needs to be kept in a group (single piranhas are more, not less, nervy) in 300L+, with sturdy tankmates or none.

A tiny, jewel-coloured nano fish suited to planted tanks and shrimp tanks alike — peaceful enough for a species tank or a very calm community. Shy at first; a well-planted tank with floating plants helps it settle and show its colours instead of hiding. Best in a group of 8 or more given its small size and shoaling nature.
common_mistakes: Housing with fast, boisterous tankmates that outcompete it for food
Keeping in a bare tank with nowhere to feel secure, so it hides constantly

care_notes: A cold-tolerant, hardy schooling fish that doesn't need a heater in most rooms, making it one of the few genuinely beginner-proof community fish. Best in a group of 6 or more, where its subtle colours and active shoaling behaviour show best. Handles a wide temperature and hardness range better than almost any other common aquarium fish.
common_mistakes: Keeping too few, so the school never settles and colours stay dull
Assuming it needs tropical heating like most other community fish

care_notes: A larger relative of the common molly with a tall, showy dorsal 'sail' fin (most visible on males). Genuinely thrives with a little aquarium salt or light brackish water, unlike most freshwater community fish — a pinch of marine salt mix is beneficial, not required, distinguishing it from the strict-brackish species on this list. Needs harder, more alkaline water and more space than a standard molly given its larger adult size.
common_mistakes: Keeping in very soft, acidic water, which mollies of any kind tend to do poorly in long-term
Underestimating adult size compared to the common molly

care_notes: A close relative of the common platy, slightly larger and noticeably more cold-tolerant, able to handle cooler unheated rooms better than most other platies and livebearers. Otherwise shares the platy's easygoing temperament and prolific livebearing — a small mixed group of females to males (2-3 females per male) avoids over-harassment of females.
common_mistakes: Keeping a single male with one female, leading to constant harassment — use a female-heavy ratio
Assuming it needs the same warmth as tropical tetras when it actually tolerates cooler water well

care_notes: A surface-dwelling livebearer with a distinctive elongated lower jaw, named for the way males spar with each other. Keep only one male per tank unless the tank is large, since males fight; needs a tight-fitting lid as it's a strong jumper. Prefers small live/floating foods it can pick from the surface over sinking flake.
common_mistakes: Keeping multiple males together in a small tank, causing ongoing fights
An open-top tank — it jumps readily

care_notes: Grows over 1m and needs pond-scale housing as an adult — a very common impulse-buy mistake as a small juvenile.
Grows very large (60cm+) and needs a correspondingly huge tank as an adult.

Sold as a small, cute juvenile but grows very large (up to 30cm) and lives decades — genuinely needs an eventual tank size and long-term commitment most buyers don't plan for. Highly social, needs a group of 6 or more or it becomes stressed and reclusive; a lone clown loach is a common and avoidable welfare problem.
common_mistakes: Buying a 5cm juvenile without researching eventual adult size and multi-decade lifespan
Keeping only 1-2, causing stress in this strongly social species
Sharp substrate that damages sensitive barbels
disputed: Adult size is often understated in shops — juveniles sold at 3-5cm can eventually reach 30cm, occasionally more, over many years.

care_notes: A social, characterful bottom-dweller that establishes a small pecking order among its own kind — keep 5 or more, never fewer than 3, or a lone/pair loach becomes stressed and reclusive. Will eat snails, useful for pest-snail control but not compatible with a deliberate mystery/nerite snail collection. Needs sand or smooth gravel — sharp substrate can damage its barbels.
common_mistakes: Keeping only 1-2, which causes stress and bullying within the small group
Mixing with a snail collection the loach will happily eat
Sharp/rough substrate that wears down sensitive barbels

care_notes: A tall-bodied cichlid prized for colour, but genuinely demanding: needs warm, soft, very clean water with frequent large water changes, and is sensitive to poor water quality and disease in a way beginner fish aren't. Best kept in a group of 6+ in a tall, spacious tank of their own or with only calm, similarly warm-water tankmates. Not a fish to add to a general community tank as an afterthought.
common_mistakes: Buying discus for a standard 25°C community tank instead of a dedicated warm, soft-water setup
Underestimating the water-change frequency needed to keep them healthy
Mixing with fin-nippers or boisterous tankmates that stress them off their food
disputed: Minimum group size is debated: some keepers succeed with a bonded pair, but 6+ is the safer recommendation to avoid one fish being bullied — we list the safer figure.

care_notes: Grows to 30-35cm and is a large, food-aggressive cichlid — needs 250L+ alone, more with tankmates. Rearranges décor and eats small tankmates.
A large, territorial hybrid cichlid, often kept alone — grows to 25-30cm and needs 200L+. Not reef/community-tank material.
A large hybrid cichlid, grows to ~20-25cm — semi-aggressive, needs 150L+.

A hardier, more temperature-tolerant alternative to the German Blue Ram — better suited to a standard community tank around 24-25°C rather than needing the warmer, softer water the German Blue Ram demands. Peaceful toward other fish, forms pairs, and does well on the substrate level of a planted community tank.
common_mistakes: Assuming it needs the same narrow, warm, soft-water conditions as the German Blue Ram — it's noticeably more forgiving

care_notes: A colourful, cave-spawning West African dwarf cichlid, generally peaceful outside of breeding — a mated pair becomes territorial and protective around a cave and fry, which can mean chasing off other bottom-dwelling tankmates during that period. Provide caves/pots as spawning sites. Hardy and adaptable to a wide range of water parameters for a cichlid.
common_mistakes: Keeping two pairs in a modest tank, inviting territorial fighting over breeding caves
Not providing a cave or similar shelter, which the female especially wants for spawning

care_notes: An African Rift Lake (Lake Malawi) cichlid needing hard, strongly alkaline water very different from most South American/Asian community fish — not compatible with a typical soft-water planted community tank. Best kept only with other Malawi cichlids of similar temperament in a species-appropriate rocky, hard-water setup, at a stocking density higher than most community tanks to spread out aggression.
common_mistakes: Mixing with soft-water community fish (tetras, corydoras, etc.) that need very different, incompatible water chemistry
Understocking a Malawi cichlid tank, which concentrates aggression onto fewer targets

care_notes: One of the hardiest, most cold-tolerant labyrinth fish, able to handle unheated rooms better than most tropicals — but genuinely aggressive, especially males toward each other and toward other long-finned or brightly-coloured fish. Best kept alone, in a male/female pair, or with robust, fast tankmates that can avoid it, not in a typical peaceful community.
common_mistakes: Adding it to a peaceful community tank expecting betta-like manageable aggression — it's considerably more pugnacious
Keeping two males together outside a very large tank

care_notes: A genuinely delicate blackwater species needing very soft, acidic, warm water and excellent water quality — a poor beginner choice despite its calm, attractive look, and not compatible with the harder, more neutral water most community fish and plants prefer. Best in a dedicated soft-water blackwater tank with tannin-stained water (driftwood, leaf litter) and calm tankmates from the same conditions.
common_mistakes: Adding it to a standard neutral-pH community tank, where it fails to thrive long-term
Underestimating how sensitive it is to fluctuating water quality compared to hardier gouramis

care_notes: A tiny, calm labyrinth fish suited to nano and heavily-planted tanks, notable for making an audible croaking/clicking sound (a real labyrinth-organ trait, not a health problem). Peaceful and easily outcompeted for food by fast, boisterous tankmates, so pair it with equally calm nano fish or shrimp rather than typical energetic community fish.
common_mistakes: Housing with fast, food-competitive tankmates that out-eat it
Mistaking its clicking sound for a filter problem rather than normal fish behaviour

care_notes: A hardy, actively-swimming schooling fish whose vivid two-tone colour intensifies with age and good care — young fish are much duller than adults, which surprises new buyers expecting instant colour. Best kept 6+ in a longer tank that gives room to swim; colours and confidence both improve in a proper-sized group.
common_mistakes: Expecting full adult colour on day one — it takes months to develop
Keeping too few or in too small/short a tank for its active swimming style

care_notes: Frequently confused in shops with the true Siamese Algae Eater, which it closely resembles — the Flying Fox becomes territorial toward its own kind and similar-shaped fish as it matures, and is a less reliable algae eater long-term. Best kept singly rather than in a group unless the tank is large.
common_mistakes: Buying it as a Siamese Algae Eater substitute expecting identical peaceful behaviour
Keeping more than one in a modest tank, inviting territorial fighting

care_notes: One of the few fish that reliably eats black beard algae, alongside general grazing and community food. Active and fast-growing, needing more swimming room than its small size suggests. Frequently confused in shops with the true SAE vs. the similar-looking, more aggressive Flying Fox or the much less useful Chinese Algae Eater — check the real Latin name before buying if algae control is the goal.
common_mistakes: Buying a 'Chinese Algae Eater' or Flying Fox expecting the same friendly algae-eating behaviour
Underestimating adult size and activity level for the tank

care_notes: Sold small as a friendly algae-eater, but grows large and territorial with age, often stops eating algae once mature and can injure slow-bodied tankmates (notably flat-sided fish like angelfish and discus) by rasping their slime coat. Rarely a good long-term community fish — the Siamese Algae Eater is the better choice for most planted community tanks.
common_mistakes: Buying it purely as a small, cute algae eater without researching adult size and temperament
Keeping it with slow, flat-bodied fish it can injure once mature

care_notes: Grows to 60cm+ and is really a pond fish, not an aquarium fish long-term.

Needs brackish (part-salt) water to thrive long-term, not a standard freshwater community tank — a common and harmful mis-sell, since juveniles of many of these species are sold in plain freshwater shop tanks and tolerate it only for a while. Research the specific salinity and adult size this species needs before buying. A fast-swimming schooling fish that needs to be kept in a real group (5+) and increasing salinity toward marine strength as it grows, alongside a large tank to match its active swimming.
common_mistakes: Keeping too few — this species is genuinely stressed and skittish alone or in pairs
Long-term freshwater housing instead of transitioning salinity upward

A genuinely mis-sold species: routinely kept in plain freshwater shop tanks as a juvenile, but needs increasing salinity as it grows and becomes fully marine as an adult. Aggressive, fin-nipping, and needs a hard, sharp-beaked diet (snails, shellfish) to wear down its ever-growing teeth — it cannot be kept with slow or long-finned tankmates.
common_mistakes: Buying it as a 'freshwater' fish because that's how the shop tank was set up
Never feeding hard-shelled food, leading to overgrown teeth that stop it eating
Housing with any other fish it can nip

Best kept alone or in a species tank, not a general community.

Never offering snails/shellfish to wear down its teeth

A small South/West Indian cichlid that does well in slightly hard, slightly alkaline water and tolerates mild brackish conditions but doesn't strictly require them, unlike many other species on this list — genuinely more freshwater-flexible. Forms pairs and can become territorial when breeding; a good species-tank or calm-community choice for hard-water setups.

Pairing with soft, acidic-water specialists it won't thrive alongside

A classic root-feeding background plant — plant it in nutrient-rich substrate (or use root tabs under gravel/sand) rather than relying on water-column dosing alone, since most of its uptake is through its roots. Grows into a large rosette over time, so give it real space; older outer leaves naturally yellow and die back and should be trimmed off. Tolerates low-to-moderate light and doesn't strictly need CO2, though it grows faster with both.
common_mistakes: Planting in bare, nutrient-poor gravel with no root tabs, then wondering why growth stalls
Underestimating final size in a small tank

care_notes: A tough, slow-growing foreground/midground plant available in green, red-brown and bronze forms. Famous for 'crypt melt' — dropping most of its leaves after being moved to a new tank or after a big change in water conditions. This is not usually fatal: leave the roots in place and it typically regrows from the base within a few weeks. Spreads slowly by runners into a nice groundcover over time.
common_mistakes: Pulling up the whole plant after 'crypt melt', assuming it died, when the roots were still alive
Rearranging the tank or dosing heavily right after planting, triggering melt unnecessarily

care_notes: A tough, slow-growing rhizome plant that, like Java Fern, must be tied to driftwood or rock rather than planted in substrate — the rhizome rots if buried. Handles low light and no CO2 comfortably, which is exactly why it's one of the most-recommended first plants. Its broad, dark leaves are prone to algae if light is too strong for the plant's slow growth rate, so keep it out of direct high light or pair with faster-growing plants that use up the excess nutrients.
common_mistakes: Burying the rhizome in substrate
Placing it under intense light meant for faster carpeting plants, inviting algae on its slow-growing leaves

care_notes: A classic low-light, no-CO2-required background plant that attaches its roots to driftwood or rock rather than growing in substrate. Slow-growing but extremely tolerant, and its tough, bitter leaves are rarely eaten by fish. New plantlets often sprout directly from the edges of older leaves — these can be cut off and tied down separately once they have a few roots.
common_mistakes: Burying the rhizome (the thick horizontal stem) in substrate — it will rot; only the roots should be buried, or better, just tie it to hardscape
Expecting fast growth — this plant is measured in months, not weeks

care_notes: A popular stem plant that turns pink-to-red under strong light and shows green under weaker light — a good, forgiving way to learn stem-plant trimming and replanting. Grows quickly, especially with CO2. Pinch the top few cm off each stem periodically and replant the cutting to keep the group bushy instead of one tall, bare-bottomed stalk.
common_mistakes: Never trimming, so the tank ends up with tall bare stems and all the leaf growth at the very top
Expecting red colour under low light — colour intensity is light-driven

care_notes: A fast-growing stem plant with distinctive lacy, variable leaf shapes (leaves grown underwater look different from ones grown emersed in the nursery — new growth after planting will look different from what you bought, which is normal). Can be planted in substrate or left floating. Its speed makes it a good nutrient-competitor against algae in a new tank. Trim and replant cuttings to keep it bushy rather than leggy.
common_mistakes: Assuming it's dying when the leaf shape changes after a few weeks underwater — that's normal adaptation, not decline
Letting it grow leggy and thin without trimming and replanting the tops

care_notes: An easy, thick-leaved stem plant that tolerates low light and no CO2, making it a reliable background choice for a first planted tank. Grows upright with rounded, succulent-looking leaves; pinch and replant the tops periodically to keep it bushy. Also sold as the herb Brahmi for human consumption — the aquarium form is the same species.
common_mistakes: Letting stems get long and bare at the base without trimming and replanting the tops

care_notes: An extremely fast-growing stem plant that has no true roots — it's usually left floating or loosely weighted rather than planted, and works equally well either way. Excellent at soaking up excess nutrients in a new or overstocked tank, which helps keep algae down. It sheds fine needle-like leaves readily, especially when moved between tanks or light levels — a bit of shedding is normal, not a sign of dying.
common_mistakes: Trying to root it deep in substrate and being confused when the buried section rots — it doesn't need substrate at all
Assuming needle-drop after a move means the plant is dead

care_notes: A fast, round-leafed stem/creeping plant that can be grown planted, floating, or trained emersed above the waterline. Tolerant of low light and no CO2, and grows quickly enough to help outcompete algae in a new tank. Roots readily from any node touching substrate or water, so cuttings establish easily.
common_mistakes: Letting it grow emersed out of an open-top tank without noticing — it will happily climb out and keep growing in air

care_notes: A rootless, fast-growing stem plant usually left loose and floating rather than planted — fry and shrimp shelter in its fine, feathery growth. Extremely undemanding: no CO2, no substrate, tolerant of a wide range of water. Multiplies quickly by fragmentation, so thin it out regularly or it can take over the surface.
common_mistakes: Letting it fill the whole surface and block light to everything below
Trying to anchor it in substrate — it's meant to float or drift loose

care_notes: A low, round-leafed carpeting plant, often used as an easier alternative to Dwarf Baby Tears. Grows well with CO2 and strong light, and can carpet even without CO2 given enough light and patience, unlike many other true carpeting plants. Plant small portions a few cm apart directly in substrate and press down gently; it spreads by runners across the surface rather than growing tall.
common_mistakes: Planting too deep, so it can't spread laterally along the substrate surface
Skipping root tabs/rich substrate — it's a moderately hungry plant

care_notes: A popular carpeting grass for the foreground. Needs bright light and consistent CO2 to carpet properly and stay short and dense — under weak light or no CO2 it grows tall and sparse instead of spreading sideways. Plant small tufts a couple of cm apart directly in substrate; it fills in via runners over several weeks. Regular trimming just above substrate encourages it to spread rather than grow upward.
common_mistakes: Expecting a dense carpet without CO2 injection and strong light — it will grow tall and thin instead
Planting too sparsely and giving up before it has time to spread via runners

care_notes: A floating plant with round, lettuce-like leaves and long trailing roots that fish and shrimp fry love to hide in. Needs no substrate or CO2, just bright light and stable surface conditions — strong surface agitation from a filter outlet can flip or drown the leaves, so give it a calmer corner. Multiplies quickly by runners; thin it out regularly or it will shade the whole tank from light.
common_mistakes: Placing it directly under strong filter outflow, where it gets flipped and waterlogged
Letting it cover the whole surface, which starves everything below of light

care_notes: The single easiest aquarium plant to grow — tolerates almost any water and low light, and needs no CO2 or substrate. Tie small clumps to driftwood, rock or a mesh with cotton thread or fine fishing line; it attaches on its own within a few weeks. Trim with scissors whenever it gets shaggy — cuttings can be tied down elsewhere and will grow into new mats. A favourite hiding/grazing spot for shrimp and fry.
common_mistakes: Planting it in substrate, where it rots — it should be tied to hardscape, not buried
Letting it grow into a thick, detritus-trapping mat without ever trimming
Expecting fast growth under very low light

care_notes: A fast-growing, grass-like background plant that spreads by runners and quickly forms a dense backdrop. Tolerates a wide range of hardness and doesn't need CO2 or intense light, making it one of the easiest tall plants for a first planted tank. Trim tall leaves that reach the surface and flop over rather than letting them shade the rest of the tank.
common_mistakes: Trimming leaves mid-blade instead of at the base, which leaves an unsightly cut edge that doesn't regrow cleanly
Restricting the substrate area, which limits how much it can spread by runners

care_notes: A fast, feathery-leafed plant that can be grown either rooted in substrate or floating — floating gives faster growth and denser cover for fry and shrimp. Undemanding about light and doesn't need CO2, though it grows faster with both. Small plantlets often form on the edges of mature leaves and can be separated once they have a few roots of their own.
common_mistakes: Planting the whole thing in substrate in a low-light tank and being disappointed by slow growth, when floating it would grow much faster

care_notes: A cheap, hardy, near-transparent shrimp often sold as 'feeder' stock but perfectly good as a display/cleanup-crew shrimp in its own right. Tougher and more tolerant of average water quality than Neocaridina/Caridina shrimp, making it a good first shrimp. Will scavenge leftover food and eat some algae/biofilm. Larger and slightly more predatory than cherry shrimp — can occasionally take very small fry.
common_mistakes: Buying it purely as fish food, then being surprised how personable and long-lived it actually is when kept properly
Expecting the same fragility/precise-parameter needs as premium ornamental shrimp — it's actually the tougher option

care_notes: A burrowing snail that spends the day under the substrate surface and emerges at night — genuinely useful for aerating and turning over substrate, preventing anaerobic dead spots, rather than a pure pest. Breeds prolifically (it's livebearing and self-fertilising, so a single snail can start a population), and is the species most associated with sudden 'snail explosions' in new tanks. An assassin snail population will bring numbers back down naturally.
common_mistakes: Panicking and trying to manually remove every snail during a population boom, when the population self-limits once excess food/waste runs out
Not realising a single snail is enough to eventually populate a whole tank

care_notes: A predatory snail kept specifically to control pest snail (pond/bladder snail) population explosions — it hunts and eats other snails, including undesirably large numbers of them. Also scavenges leftover food and won't touch healthy plants. Breeds much more slowly than pest snails, so its population stays naturally in check once pest snails run low. Needs harder, more alkaline water than many fish — soft, acidic water erodes its shell.
common_mistakes: Adding it expecting it to also leave your deliberately-kept mystery/nerite snails alone — it will eat those too, given the chance
Soft/acidic water that thins and pits the shell over time
